There are countries that handle the internet in a much more reasonable, libertarian manner.

There are two types of ISPs. The first gets a monopoly (since we don't want every ISP trenching in front of every house). Their rate is set by the government, and is designed to ensure a small but sufficient profit from providing a pipe.

The second type of ISP does not have a monopoly. They can do whatever the heck they want, and they buy access from the monopolies at wholesale rates. Those ISPs can throttle, filter, whatever, and you are free to pick whatever one you want whatever policy you want. Without a monopoly, the market means you can find lots of alternatives.

That's how the internet started in the US, with dial-up. The phone company, who was a monopoly, was regulated. They got immunity from lawsuits for facilitating criminal behaviour, and in exchange for their monopoly, they were prevented from discriminating on the basis of content. They couldn't charge Republicans $10,000 a month for their phone line, or force businesses that needed a phone to function tens of thousands just because the market would bear it.

Anyone who wanted to could become an ISP - you just hooked up some modems to the phone line. Anyone could select any ISP they wanted, with whatever price or rules they wanted. The phone company was not free to disconnect you or charge you more for internet traffic vs phone traffic.

The monopoly was regulated, non-monopolies were not. The monopoly could even play if they wanted to - nothing stopped AT&T from being an ISP, and I was one of their customers for years on AT&T WorldNet. They had affordable pricing, no throttling, wouldn't kick you off for using too much, and were as fast as FCC regulations allowed.

Long distance was similar - phone companies could be long distance companies if they wanted, but by law, you were free to choose any long distance company you wanted. They had monopolies on local calls (since running dozens of services to everyone's house would cause problems), at fixed and reasonable rates. Long distance didn't have to run along your wires, and so they had to give access at their locations to companies that wanted to run the long distance calls themselves.
